brief.head: Planner, meet doer
brief.text: Ajay Shah splits him­self in two: a plan­ner who sets pri­or­i­ties, and a doer who ex­e­cutes one task fully, miss­ing other dead­lines if need be. {091-C01}

brief.head: The fear test
brief.text: Is there any­one in your coun­try you are afraid of? If so, Ajay Shah said, that per­son has ar­bi­trary power, and some­thing is wrong. {091-C05}

brief.head: Rules beat norms
brief.text: Norms do real work, Ajay Shah said, but only checks writ­ten into law or the Constitution sur­vive pres­sure. Anything else “can just get whisked away in no time”. {091-C08}

brief.head: Courts have caught up
brief.text: SEBI’s founders put a judge in­side the reg­u­la­tor in 1992, doubt­ing the Bombay High Court. XKDR Forum’s work, Ajay Shah said, shows such courts are now rea­son­ably ef­fi­cient. {091-S06}

brief.head: Who judges the judges
brief.text: Not min­is­ters or MPs, Ajay Shah said, cit­ing the law aca­demic Tarunabh Khaitan. A judge’s real check is the re­spect of peers, lawyers, law blog­gers and jour­nals. {091-C12}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on dividing the state
lead.head: No kings, please, we’re a republic

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 91

body: Many peo­ple be­have as if democ­racy is all about vot­ing, Amit Varma said.
Ajay Shah’s reply set the agenda for the hour. “The essence of democ­racy is not elec­tions,” he said. “It is in checks and bal­ances. It is in dis­per­sion of power.” {091-C02}

Voting, in his ac­count, only chooses who plays the leg­isla­tive role. Use it to choose a king and the king could never be un­seated, be­cause how could any­one or­gan­ise an op­po­si­tion party against a king?

The hosts had cov­ered one way of spread­ing power, de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion, in an ear­lier episode. This one took up the sec­ond: three co-equal branches, a leg­is­la­ture that writes laws, an ex­ec­u­tive that im­ple­ments them and a ju­di­ciary that set­tles con­flicts.
## Kings and char­ters
Shah began in the bad old days, when the Emperor Aurangzeb’s power was com­plete. Rome made the first break: a re­pub­lic where about fifty fam­i­lies spread power out and set up judges.

The story restarted in England in 1215, when mer­chants and fi­nance peo­ple seized King John. “They put a knife to his throat and they forced him to sign,” Shah said. The doc­u­ment was the Magna Carta. {091-S01}
From there the road ran through Oliver Cromwell to Montesquieu, who pro­posed cut­ting the state into three. The clear­est ex­pres­sion came, Shah said, in Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution.

He made it con­crete with a speech of­fence. Legislators de­cide whether it is a crime; the po­lice only in­ves­ti­gate; only a judge, after hear­ing both sides, de­cides on pun­ish­ment. “To write a law, you gotta win elec­tions,” he said. {091-C03}
As “a stupid econ­o­mist”, Shah con­fessed, it took him years to see how pow­er­ful this was, be­cause econ­o­mists tend to pic­ture gov­ern­ment as one mono­lithic thing.
## The Indian de­tour

India began dif­fer­ently. In the Constituent Assembly, Babasaheb Ambedkar agreed the ju­di­ciary must stand apart, but saw no great loss in not sep­a­rat­ing the ex­ec­u­tive from the leg­is­la­ture in the American way.

Two later shifts, Varma said, made things worse: Indira Gandhi’s cen­tral­i­sa­tion of power within par­ties, and the anti-defection law of the late 1980s, which made every MP vote as the whip says. Of the law he said: “Don’t look at in­ten­tion, look at out­come.”

The re­sult, in Shah’s phrase, is the ad­min­is­tra­tive state, “a world where of­fi­cials of the ex­ec­u­tive branch dis­pro­por­tion­ately exert leg­isla­tive and ju­di­cial pow­ers”. No coun­try, he said, has it worse than India. {091-C06}

Regulators re­peat the pat­tern in minia­ture. At SEBI, Shah said, one body writes the rules, in­ves­ti­gates, pros­e­cutes and judges: “And the judge and the pros­e­cu­tor and the in­ves­ti­ga­tor go have lunch to­gether.” {091-S05}
## Room for hope

Still, Shah was op­ti­mistic. Separation of pow­ers was miss­ing from the orig­i­nal text, he said, but it has en­tered India’s liv­ing con­sti­tu­tion through the Supreme Court’s basic struc­ture doc­trine.
America, mean­while, is push­ing back: in 2024 its Supreme Court largely struck down Chevron def­er­ence.
Varma’s worry was at­ro­phy: a party long in power can fill every in­sti­tu­tion with its own peo­ple. The task, he said, is done only when a constitution’s val­ues per­co­late through so­ci­ety.
Shah agreed that noth­ing can be taken for granted, and that in India the in­stinct is still to look for a strong­man.
The state, he had said ear­lier, was never meant to be cosy: “This is not a happy fam­ily. This is not a har­mo­nious fam­ily. It’s a game of con­flict.”

second.label: Party democracy
second.head: Shastri says no to Nehru
second.deck: Amit Varma on the Babri idol and a Congress that once argued
body: When the Ram idol was placed in­side the Babri Masjid, Jawaharlal Nehru, in Delhi, or­dered it re­moved within a cou­ple of days, be­fore things got out of hand. {091-S03}

But UP’s chief min­is­ter was Govind Ballabh Pant, and his deputy, Lal Bahadur Shastri, who would have had to carry out the order, re­fused. In that case, Amit Varma said, he wishes they had obeyed Nehru.

His point was about the Congress of the 1950s and 1960s, a grand tent where local politi­cians could defy the cen­tre and the local party chose its chief min­is­ter. That ended in the 1970s, when Indira Gandhi cen­tralised power and the high com­mand began ap­point­ing chief min­is­ters. {#indira}

quote.text: Before this you couldn’t freak­ing ap­point a chief min­is­ter, the local party would de­cide it

third.head: Chevron runs out of gas

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on America’s retreat from Chevron deference

body: Under Roosevelt, Ajay Shah said, the US fed­eral gov­ern­ment built agency upon agency. Nervous Republicans an­swered with the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946, a sin­gle rule­book for every fed­eral agency. {091-C11}

Court or­ders in a case in­volv­ing the oil com­pany Chevron later cre­ated Chevron def­er­ence. If an agency ex­pert had ap­plied her mind and drafted a reg­u­la­tion, judges could re­view only the process, not the sub­stance. Many saw that as leg­isla­tive power seep­ing into the ad­min­is­tra­tive state. {091-S07}
In 2024 the US Supreme Court largely struck it down. “You may be the best ex­pert in the world, you may have 15 PhDs,” Shah said, “but a judge can re­open a mat­ter.”
In a sec­ond case, some­one ar­gued that the SEC’s in-house judge de­nied him a jury trial; the Supreme Court struck that ar­range­ment down as un­con­sti­tu­tional.

from1.head: No kings, please, we’re a republic

quote.text: It would be a very sad world in which vot­ing was used to choose a king.

box.title: The thinker behind the idea
box.text: Montesquieu, Ajay Shah said, drew on ear­lier thinkers to pro­pose cut­ting the state ver­ti­cally into three pieces: leg­is­la­ture, ex­ec­u­tive and ju­di­ciary. Each would keep to its own lane and check the oth­ers. Shah placed him in the 17th cen­tury. {#montesquieu}

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: Votes don’t make a democracy
sections.caption: democracy as dispersion of power
body: Amit Varma framed the sub­ject with a com­mon be­lief: that democ­racy is all about vot­ing. People go to a booth, se­lect a can­di­date, and the can­di­date rules over them.

Ajay Shah went fur­ther. At heart, he said, democ­racy is about dis­per­sion of power and checks and bal­ances. Voting is just a way of choos­ing the peo­ple who will play a leg­isla­tive role. {091-C02}
Used to choose a king, it would pro­duce a ruler im­pos­si­ble to un­seat, be­cause no­body could or­gan­ise an op­po­si­tion party against a king.
## Two grand ideas

One way to dis­perse power, Shah said, is de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion, cov­ered in an ear­lier episode: under the sub­sidiar­ity prin­ci­ple, each func­tion goes to the low­est level of gov­ern­ment that can han­dle it, with only a few, like for­eign pol­icy and mil­i­tary af­fairs, left to the union.

The sec­ond is sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers. The state is not a mono­lithic or­gan­i­sa­tion but three co-equal branches: a leg­is­la­ture that writes laws, an ex­ec­u­tive that im­ple­ments them and a ju­di­ciary that looks at a con­flict and puts out an order. None can over­ride the oth­ers.
People who yearn for a strong­man, Shah said, find these three branches ir­ri­tat­ing. But that, he said, is sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers.

~ The episode opened with Shah’s per­sonal ver­sion of the idea: a plan­ner who plans, then a doer who only does. Varma ad­mired it, while ad­mit­ting that in his case the plan­ner rocks but the doer is “a frickin’ nikamma”. {#nikamma}

quote.text: It would be a very sad world in which vot­ing was used to choose a king.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: From Aurangzeb to Article 3
sections.caption: how power was prised from kings
body: Ajay Shah started with ab­so­lute monar­chy: if the Emperor Aurangzeb or­dered someone’s head off, there was no choice, and kings al­lied with re­li­gion, as when the Pope crowned Napoleon. {091-J02}

Rome’s re­pub­lic, the world’s first, spread power out until, in Shah’s words, it “was de­stroyed by the great man Julius Caesar”. {091-J03} England restarted the story with the Magna Carta in 1215, a road that led to Oliver Cromwell and the be­head­ing of Charles I.
## Three lanes

Then came Montesquieu, whom Shah placed in the 17th cen­tury. His pro­posal was to cut the state ver­ti­cally into a leg­is­la­ture, an ex­ec­u­tive and a ju­di­ciary, each in its own lane. {#montesquieu}

Shah’s ex­am­ple was a speech of­fence under the Indian Penal Code. Legislators de­cide whether it is a crime. {091-C03} Police in­ves­ti­gate against the writ­ten law. The judge alone de­cides on pun­ish­ment, and can­not go after any­one on her own ini­tia­tive. He called this a mind-blowing achieve­ment in po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy.

Amit Varma added that in the US one per­son in­ves­ti­gates and an­other de­cides whether to pros­e­cute. That, Shah said, bor­row­ing David Friedman’s phrase, is the ma­chin­ery of free­dom. {091-R01}
~ The ideas found their clear­est ex­pres­sion in Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution, which set up three co-equal branches with no fear of each other.

quote.text: It was a great day for mankind when these con­cepts were fig­ured out.

sections.label: The Indian story
sections.head: The executive takes the wheel
sections.caption: India’s executive-heavy state
body: India’s Constituent Assembly de­bated the ques­tion, Ajay Shah said. Professor K.T. Shah moved a res­o­lu­tion, Article 40A, for a clear sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers. Babasaheb Ambedkar replied that the ex­ec­u­tive must be sep­a­rate from the ju­di­ciary, but saw no great loss in not sep­a­rat­ing it from the leg­is­la­ture. {091-S02}
Amit Varma urged that the choice be judged in con­text, when the coun­try was fall­ing apart and today’s map did not yet exist.
## The whip hand
Then came the anti-defection law of the late 1980s. Meant to stop horse-trading, it made every MP vote as the whip says. Varma’s ver­dict: “You could run par­lia­ment from an Excel sheet.” {091-J06}
Power within par­ties, he added, had al­ready been cen­tralised under Indira Gandhi. Together these let a rul­ing party run both the ex­ec­u­tive and the leg­is­la­ture from the top. {#combine}

With no MP both­er­ing to read bills, Shah said, the joint sec­re­tary writes the law, and dis­trict col­lec­tors dou­ble as dis­trict mag­is­trates, a British legacy from when courts were scarce. This is the ad­min­is­tra­tive state. {091-C06}

~ His hope lies in the basic struc­ture doc­trine, through which sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers has en­tered India’s liv­ing con­sti­tu­tion, though a plain read­ing of the text would not find it. {091-C09}

quote.text: There is no dis­pute what­so­ever that the ex­ec­u­tive should be sep­a­rated from the ju­di­ciary.
quote.who: Babasaheb Ambedkar, as read by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The regulators
sections.head: A small state inside SEBI
sections.caption: SEBI’s three branches under one roof
body: Before the chap­ter, Amit Varma re­minded Ajay Shah, “ex­plic­itly for the cam­era”, to be kind. {091-J07} Shah, who enor­mously re­spects SEBI’s founders, in­clud­ing Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain, still called the orig­i­nal SEBI Act “a re­ally bad piece of work”.
The RBI was cre­ated in 1934, mostly as a mon­e­tary au­thor­ity, Shah said; SEBI came in 1992 and copied many of its prac­tices. {#rbi}
## A state in minia­ture
A regulator’s reg­u­la­tions are laws writ­ten by un­elected of­fi­cials, Shah said, and the SEBI Act suf­fered from what is called ex­ces­sive del­e­ga­tion. {091-C10}

SEBI also in­ves­ti­gates and pros­e­cutes, with the roles mixed up, and then a SEBI em­ployee plays judge. {091-S05} Early or­ders sim­ply de­clared some­one guilty and im­posed a fine of, say, ₹10 crore, with no rea­son­ing. Appeals went to the DEA sec­re­tary, who sat on SEBI’s board.

Elsewhere it is cleaner. In Britain and under Australia’s twin-peaks model, the reg­u­la­tor builds a case and takes it to a court or tri­bunal. At the US SEC, the ad­min­is­tra­tive law judge sits in­side the build­ing but be­longs to the ju­di­ciary.

~ SEBI’s founders put a judge in­side in 1992 be­cause they thought the Bombay High Court would never get any­thing done. XKDR Forum’s re­cent work, Shah said, shows the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now rea­son­ably ef­fi­cient, so the trade-offs may have changed. {091-S06}

quote.text: Regulations are laws. So here you have un­elected of­fi­cials who are draft­ing law

sections.label: The American turn
sections.head: Even the model needs mending
sections.caption: America’s pushback on its agencies
body: Amit Varma asked whether America, so often the model, had al­ways got sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers right. Ajay Shah called the field red hot; the Emerging Markets Conference had held an en­tire ses­sion on it. {091-R07}
Under Roosevelt, the fed­eral gov­ern­ment built agen­cies upon agen­cies, with Democrats lead­ing the charge. Nervous Republicans pushed for the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946.
## One rule­book

Shah called the APA “a phe­nom­e­nal piece of work”: a sin­gle law set­ting out checks and bal­ances for every fed­eral agency. The draft Indian Financial Code, on which he worked, did the same, with about 140 sec­tions bind­ing RBI, SEBI and a debt man­age­ment agency alike. {091-C11}

Varma had ear­lier pre­dicted that Perplexity could re­pro­duce Shah’s out­line. The APA, Shah shot back, is slim but must be read with the thou­sands of court or­ders that fol­lowed: a law the tool could not parse alone. {091-J08}

Those or­ders pro­duced Chevron def­er­ence, which stopped judges ques­tion­ing the sub­stance of an expert’s reg­u­la­tion. In 2024 the Supreme Court largely struck it down. {091-S07} Separately, it found the SEC’s in-house tri­als un­con­sti­tu­tional after some­one de­manded a jury.
~ Varma took heart from both rul­ings: they showed, he said, that you can ac­tu­ally move in the right di­rec­tion.

quote.text: It is one sin­gle law that ap­plies to all fed­eral agen­cies.

sections.label: The afterthoughts
sections.head: Every generation, a new fight
sections.caption: atrophy, vigilance and culture
body: Amit Varma’s worry was at­ro­phy. A well-designed sys­tem, he said, de­cays as pol­i­tics and in­cen­tives take over, and a party long in power can fill every in­sti­tu­tion with its own peo­ple.
Still, sep­a­ra­tion adds fric­tion. “But when it comes to the state, fric­tion is a good thing,” Varma said: a process guar­an­tees that noth­ing hasty will be done. {#friction}
It also makes a power grab vis­i­ble. When Indira Gandhi im­posed the Emergency, he said, no­body could pre­tend democ­racy was going on. {#emergency}
Hence, in Jefferson’s al­leged words, the need for eter­nal vig­i­lance. {#vigilance}
## Downstream of cul­ture

Varma also warned against treat­ing the Indian Constitution, “well in­ten­tioned but deeply flawed”, like a holy book. Politics, he said, quot­ing Andrew Breitbart, is down­stream of cul­ture: lib­erty lasts when every cit­i­zen in­stinc­tively ob­jects when­ever free­dom is in­fringed. {091-J15}

Ajay Shah agreed that every gen­er­a­tion has to fight its own bat­tles. He re­called Angela Merkel say­ing Germany’s true soul would be known only when the last peo­ple who lived through the Second World War had died. In re­cent elec­tions, he noted, 20 per cent voted for the AfD.
~ For judges, Shah said, the check should be not min­is­ters but peers, lawyers, law blog­gers and jour­nals, an ar­gu­ment he cred­ited to the law aca­demic Tarunabh Khaitan. {091-C12}

quote.text: The task of gov­er­nance and de­sign­ing a sys­tem is not done when you write a con­sti­tu­tion.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on atrophy, vigilance and culture

quote.text: You and me as the peo­ple should never be scared of a per­son. If you’re scared of some­body, there’s some­thing wrong in your coun­try be­cause that some­body has ar­bi­trary power.

p3.title: Tales of power
p3.deck: Kings, framers, regulators and committees: the episode’s stories, and what they teach

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how humanity learned to shrink the king
stories.head: A knife at King John’s throat
body: Ajay Shah began in the bad old days of monar­chy, when a ruler’s power was com­plete. If the Emperor Aurangzeb said off with his head, there was no ap­peal. Kings al­lied with re­li­gion, as when the Pope crowned Napoleon.

The first break came in Rome. There, Shah said, about fifty fam­i­lies took power from con­cen­trated monar­chy, spread it out and set up judges. It was the world’s first ex­per­i­ment with a re­pub­lic, and it “was de­stroyed by the great man Julius Caesar”. {091-J03}
The story restarted in England in 1215. King John was de­mand­ing crazy taxes and loans from a group of mer­chants and fi­nance peo­ple, and they seized him.

“They put a knife to his throat and they forced him to sign a doc­u­ment,” Shah said. The doc­u­ment was the Magna Carta, the Great Charter, the world’s first clear state­ment of lim­its on the power of a king. {091-S01}
Read today, he ad­mit­ted, it seems fos­silised. The lan­guage is ar­chaic, and it seems to do a few flimsy things. “But you know what? It’s 1215.”

From there the British chipped away at the king’s power through Parliament, until Oliver Cromwell and the be­head­ing of Charles I. People watched, Shah said, and un­der­stood that not hav­ing an ab­so­lute au­thor­ity is a good thing.

~ That set philoso­phers de­bat­ing how to build a state with checks and bal­ances. It led to Montesquieu’s pro­posal to cut the state in three, and fi­nally to Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution.
stories.why: Limits on power were ex­tracted, not gifted, and each step built on peo­ple see­ing the last one work. Separation of pow­ers, in Shah’s telling, is the ma­ture form of a cen­turies-old project: no­body should be a king. {091-C05}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma noted that Aristotle also de­scribed three branches of gov­ern­ment, but as func­tions of the state, not a sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how the king’s power was limited

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a regulator that holds all three powers
stories.head: Three branches, one canteen
body: SEBI was cre­ated in 1992 by founders Ajay Shah enor­mously re­spects, among them Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain. But it copied prac­tices from the RBI and ended up with all three branches of the state under one roof. {091-S05}

It drafts reg­u­la­tions, which are laws writ­ten by un­elected of­fi­cials. It in­ves­ti­gates and pros­e­cutes, with the two roles mixed up. Then a SEBI em­ployee plays judge, and his col­league is the pros­e­cu­tor.
“And the judge and the pros­e­cu­tor and the in­ves­ti­ga­tor go have lunch to­gether,” Shah said, “and they con­duct a lit­tle trial.”

~ Early or­ders sim­ply found some­one guilty and im­posed a fine of, say, ₹10 crore, with no rea­son­ing. Appeals went to the DEA sec­re­tary, a SEBI board mem­ber. India, Shah reck­ons, is about 30 per cent of the way to fix­ing it. {#thirty}
stories.why: Without sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers, a reg­u­la­tor qui­etly be­comes a minia­ture state. The clean de­sign, Shah said, stops the reg­u­la­tor at in­ves­ti­gat­ing and de­cid­ing whether to pros­e­cute, then hands the case to a real judge. {#clean}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on SEBI’s judge, prosecutor and investigator

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah reads Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly
stories.head: No great loss, said Ambedkar
body: The Constituent Assembly de­bated sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers, Ajay Shah said. Professor K.T. Shah moved a res­o­lu­tion, Article 40A, to write a clear sep­a­ra­tion into the Constitution.

Shah read out the reply of Babasaheb Ambedkar, the assembly’s in­tel­lec­tual lu­mi­nary. There was no dis­pute, Ambedkar said, that the ex­ec­u­tive should be sep­a­rated from the ju­di­ciary. But many Americans were dis­sat­is­fied with their own rigid sep­a­ra­tion of ex­ec­u­tive and leg­is­la­ture.

The work of Parliament, he ar­gued, was so com­pli­cated and vast that its mem­bers needed di­rect guid­ance from the ex­ec­u­tive sit­ting among them. He saw no very great loss, then, in not adopt­ing the American method. {091-S02}

~ So India began with no mean­ing­ful sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers. Amit Varma asked for con­text: a coun­try fall­ing apart, its map not yet drawn. The aim, he said, is to learn, not to pass judg­ment on per­son­al­i­ties.
stories.why: India’s ex­ec­u­tive-heavy state was no ac­ci­dent: its most re­spected framer chose it de­lib­er­ately, and gave rea­sons. The re­sult, Shah said, was that India grew up as a state with ex­treme ex­ec­u­tive power. {#executive}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Ambedkar’s reply to K.T. Shah

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a check that lived only in custom
stories.head: A good habit, never written down
body: Many peo­ple un­der­stood, Ajay Shah said, that a joint sec­re­tary writ­ing the laws was a farce. So, start­ing with Shivraj Patil, a norm grew of send­ing im­por­tant bills to par­lia­men­tary stand­ing com­mit­tees. {#patil}
When Shah was in the Ministry of Finance, the Speaker would refer a bill to a com­mit­tee if it drew sig­nif­i­cant crit­i­cism. No vote was needed.

The com­mit­tees had rul­ing and op­po­si­tion MPs and were al­ways chaired by the op­po­si­tion. They de­bated bills, sum­moned ex­pert wit­nesses and ques­tioned the civil ser­vants who drafted them. Shah, often an ex­pert wit­ness him­self, counts them among the good things be­hind India’s growth from 1991 to 2011.
~ But the prac­tice was never writ­ten into the rules. {091-S04} Today, he said, there is re­ally no check and bal­ance around these things.

quote.text: It was fab­u­lous. It was a great in­sti­tu­tion. Unfortunately, it was only in norms.

stories.postscript: The les­son, Shah said, is James Buchanan’s pub­lic choice rea­son­ing: these things “have to be coded in rules”. {091-C08}

quiz.q: What, according to Ajay Shah, is the essence of democracy, if not elections?
quiz.a: Checks and bal­ances and the dis­per­sion of power; vot­ing only picks leg­is­la­tors.

quiz.q: Who was demanding crazy taxes and loans when merchants put a knife to his throat?
quiz.a: King John of England, who was forced to sign the Magna Carta in 1215.

quiz.q: Which law, by Amit Varma’s account, lets you run Parliament from an Excel sheet?
quiz.a: The anti-defection law of the late 1980s, which makes MPs vote as the whip says.

quiz.q: What American term does Shah use for officials wielding legislative and judicial powers?
quiz.a: The ad­min­is­tra­tive state, and he says no coun­try has it worse than India.

quiz.q: Through which Supreme Court doctrine did separation of powers enter India’s living constitution?
quiz.a: The basic struc­ture doc­trine, the amend­ment-proof core of the Constitution built by judges.

quiz.q: What did the US Supreme Court largely strike down in 2024?
quiz.a: Chevron def­er­ence, which stopped judges ques­tion­ing the sub­stance of an agency’s reg­u­la­tions.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 91. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: B. R. shelf.title: The Machinery of Freedom
shelf.creator: David Friedman
shelf.why: Amit calls it a mag­nif­i­cent and very lib­er­tar­ian book.

shelf.title: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case for sub­sidiar­ity in a coun­try as large and var­ied as India: do as lit­tle as pos­si­ble at the Union level and push power down to cities, where peo­ple can see and talk to the of­fi­cials re­spon­si­ble for their side­walks.

shelf.title: Why I Am a Free Speech Absolutist (Episode 88, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s case for free speech: why the Indian Constitution doesn’t re­ally pro­tect it, why Nehru’s First Amendment was a mis­take to be un­der­stood in con­text, and why le­git­i­macy needs an open mar­ket­place of ideas.

shelf.title: The Anti-Defection Law (Episode 13, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra
shelf.why: Barun Mitra on how a well-meant law to stop horse-trading turned MPs into votes that fol­low the whip, one of the things Amit sees get­ting in the way of Indian democ­racy.

shelf.title: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with MR Madhavan
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with MR Madhavan on how India’s par­lia­men­tary rules, es­pe­cially the anti-defection law, weaken its democ­racy.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: Emerging Markets Conference
shelf.why: A con­fer­ence Ajay val­ues be­cause knowl­edge and ideas mat­ter there rather than a ‘great lineup of fa­mous people’; a re­cent edi­tion had a whole ses­sion on the red-hot field of the US ad­min­is­tra­tive state.

shelf.title: Administrative Procedure Act (1946)
shelf.why: The 1946 US law that binds every fed­eral agency to a sin­gle rule­book, which Ajay calls a bril­liant blue­print for checks and bal­ances on reg­u­la­tors and the same idea as India’s draft Indian Financial Code.

shelf.title: XKDR Forum’s paper on Indian courts
shelf.creator: XKDR Forum
shelf.why: It weak­ens the 1992 ar­gu­ment for giv­ing SEBI its own in-house judg­ing.

shelf.title: Chocolate by Manam
shelf.creator: Manam Chocolate
shelf.why: A Hyderabad com­pany mak­ing ex­pen­sive, re­ally good choco­late.

shelf.title: Introduction to Modern Climate Change
shelf.creator: Andrew E Dessler
shelf.why: Ajay sees cli­mate change as one of the great crises of the mod­ern world, along­side pop­ulism.

shelf.title: IPCC reports
shelf.creator: IPCC
shelf.why: Ajay usu­ally finds re­ports by in­ter­na­tional bod­ies such as the World Bank and IMF bland, be­cause they are writ­ten by com­mit­tee.

shelf.title: Fateful Choices
shelf.creator: Ian Kershaw
shelf.why: It shows how Churchill and Roosevelt worked to bring America into the Second World War on the Allied side.

shelf.title: Ten Years Gone
shelf.creator: Led Zeppelin
shelf.why: Ajay’s pick for the great­est Led Zeppelin song that is not widely known.

shelf.title: Tangerine
shelf.creator: Led Zeppelin
shelf.why: Years ago he came across the lyrics be­fore hear­ing it and won­dered what kind of song they would make.

shelf.title: I’m Gonna Crawl
shelf.creator: Led Zeppelin
shelf.why: Ajay con­sid­ers it one of the great things Plant, Page, John Paul Jones and Bonzo ever did, made at the peak of their pow­ers just be­fore the band ended.

laughs.text: Amit on Ajay’s plan­ner-doer frame­work: ‘Amit the plan­ner rocks… but Amit the doer is a frickin’ nikamma.’ Then he adds a third self: ‘there’s Amit the re­gret­ter… I could have been a con­tender.’
Ajay on ab­so­lute monar­chy: ‘If Aurangzeb said that off with his head, then Mr. Beer Biceps would have no choice.’
Ajay’s dry jab at strong­man wor­ship: Rome’s re­pub­lic, the world’s first, ‘was de­stroyed by the great man Julius Caesar.’

Ajay on how econ­o­mists pic­ture gov­ern­ment: ‘you don’t have some Aurangzeb and you’re sup­posed to go whis­per in Aurangzeb’s ears that dude, we should do in­fla­tion tar­get­ing.’ Amit prom­ises view­ers an on-screen car­toon of ex­actly that: ‘What even are these im­ages you are putting in my head?’

Amit, over­joyed that Ajay cited David Friedman: a very lib­er­tar­ian book ‘which I did not ex­pect from the se­cret statist… I’ve fi­nally found a kin­dred soul.’ Ajay replies: ‘my heart sees the ma­chin­ery of free­dom, but my head has worked out all the com­pro­mises.’

Amit on what the anti-defection law did to Parliament: ‘you could run par­lia­ment from an Excel sheet. You don’t even need peo­ple to show up. Frankly, you don’t even need to elect in­di­vid­ual leg­is­la­tors.’

Amit, after being promised six rec­om­men­da­tions and get­ting seven (‘a big bonus’), says Ajay’s pitch for IPCC re­ports (a clutch of mod­els, look at all the pic­tures, it will change how you see the world) ap­plies equally to a teenager dis­cov­er­ing the Sports Illustrated swim­suit edi­tion. ‘But you’ve been a dif­fer­ent kind of teenager, I guess.’
Max Weber’s def­i­ni­tion of the state, via Ajay: ‘a com­mu­nity that cre­ates and main­tains a mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence.’
Jefferson’s ‘al­leged words’ on eter­nal vig­i­lance as the price of free­dom, which Amit in­vokes against the slow decay of in­sti­tu­tions.
Andrew Breitbart’s ‘pol­i­tics is down­stream of culture’, which Amit uses to argue that the deeper bat­tle for lib­erty is cul­tural.
